opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me most is that Yann is genuinely fearless about his own convictions. He's held certain beliefs for decades, about neural networks, about learning from the world, about what intelligence actually requires, and he held them even when the whole field thought he was wrong. Back when neural nets were out of fashion, he kept going. That kind of persistence is rare, and it's not stubbornness for its own sake. It comes from thinking very deeply and from first principles.

He's also very honest. He says what he thinks, publicly, even when it's unpopular. You see it in his debates about large language models and AGI. A lot of people find that provocative, but I find it refreshing. In a field where so many people follow the hype or optimize for what sounds good, he's willing to say, "I don't think this is the path, and here's why." Whether or not you agree with him, it forces you to think harder.

On a personal level, he's surprisingly playful and curious. He loves music, he builds things, he flies model airplanes, he gets excited about all kinds of science outside AI. He doesn't carry himself like a legend. When you talk research with him, he treats you as a peer and engages with the idea itself, not with who you are. For a younger researcher that matters a lot. It makes you feel you're allowed to have bold ideas too.

So I'd say it's the combination: a long-term, almost idealistic vision of what intelligence should be, the courage to stand by it, and a very human, curious personality underneath. That's something I'd like to carry into my own work.

r001.rationale: The response describes Yann as persistent, honest, playful, and curious, but does not convey Kaiming’s characterization that he retained his sixteen-year-old spirit into his sixties.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what I love about Yann is how real he is. He doesn't manage himself. He just says what he thinks, and he's completely comfortable being wrong in public if that's where the argument leads. That was true when I first met him at Facebook AI Research, back when I joined as a research scientist, and it's still true now.

I think a lot of people only see him on Twitter, arguing with everyone, and they read that as arrogance. But when you actually work with him, it's the opposite. He's one of the most curious people I've ever met. If a PhD student walks up to him with a half-baked idea, he'll engage with it seriously. He doesn't care about your title. He cares whether the idea is interesting.

The other thing is his consistency. He's been saying some version of the same thing for decades. Self-supervised learning, world models, learning from observation like a baby does. In the early days, nobody wanted to hear about convolutional nets. He kept going. Then when everybody jumped on large language models, he stayed skeptical and kept pushing his own direction. You can disagree with him, and I sometimes do, but you always know where he stands. There's no politics in it.

And he's generous. At FAIR he really built a culture where people could do open, long-term research and publish everything. Many of us, including me, benefited from that enormously. I think that's underappreciated. He's a scientist first, and he genuinely wants the field to move forward, not just his own lab.

So I'd say it's the combination: brutally direct, intellectually stubborn in the good sense, and at the same time very open and generous with people. That's a rare mix.

r001.rationale: The response describes Yann as direct, curious, consistent, and generous, but does not convey Kaiming’s characterization of him retaining his sixteen-year-old spirit into his sixties.

astra-6.text: What attracts me most is his intellectual independence. Yann is willing to question assumptions, even when everybody else seems to agree on them. And he’s willing to put his own ideas out there and have people challenge them. That combination—having a strong conviction while being open to a real debate—is something I really admire. You don’t have to agree with every conclusion to appreciate that spirit.

r001.rationale: The response praises Yann’s intellectual independence and openness to debate, but does not characterize him as retaining his sixteen-year-old spirit into his sixties.
